questions.q: What does it mean for a filter condition to be "selective" in Salesforce's query optimizer?
options: It only runs during business hours
It only applies to custom objects, never standard objects
It always returns exactly one record
It's estimated to match a small enough fraction of the object's total records that using an index is worth it
questions.explain: Selectivity is about how narrow a slice of the object's rows a filter is expected to match — narrow enough, and the optimizer judges an index worth using; too broad, and it won't bother.

questions.q: Why is the custom-index selectivity threshold stricter than the standard-index threshold?
options: Custom indexes don't actually exist and this is a common misconception
Custom indexes are a documented Salesforce design choice that requires a narrower, more selective filter before the optimizer will use them, roughly 10%/5% versus the standard index's roughly 30%/15%
Custom indexes are always slower than standard indexes regardless of selectivity
There is no difference — both indexes use identical thresholds
questions.explain: Salesforce's published guidance treats custom indexes as needing a narrower filter (roughly 10% of the first million records, 5% beyond) compared to standard indexes (roughly 30%/15%) before the optimizer will use them.

questions.q: A filter uses `LIKE '%smith%'` against an indexed Name field. Why does this fail to be selective, regardless of how few records actually contain "smith"?
options: Because Name fields can never be filtered on at all
Because LIKE operators are only allowed in reports, not SOQL
Because a leading wildcard means the match could start anywhere in the value, and the index (ordered by the start of the value) can't be used to narrow that search
Because wildcards automatically disable all indexes org-wide
questions.explain: An index is ordered by the beginning of a field's value, so a leading wildcard search can't use that ordering to narrow the search — the optimizer treats it as unselective no matter how rare the actual matching value is.

questions.q: Which of these filter patterns is explicitly called out as unselective, even when the field itself is indexed?
options: A negative operator such as != or NOT LIKE
An equality filter on an indexed picklist field with a rare value
A range filter on an indexed date field
An IN clause with a short, specific list of indexed field values
questions.explain: Negative operators (!=, NOT LIKE, EXCLUDES) require evaluating what a value isn't, which an index can't shortcut, so they're treated as unselective regardless of the field's indexing or the real-world rarity of the excluded value.

questions.q: A business requirement genuinely needs a negative filter condition (e.g., Status__c != 'Closed') against an LDV-scale object. What does this lesson recommend as a practical mitigation?
options: Remove all indexes from the object so the optimizer behaves consistently
Switch the object to a Big Object, which ignores selectivity rules entirely
There is no mitigation — negative filters can never be used on LDV-scale objects for any reason
Add an additional, genuinely selective condition alongside the negative filter, even if logically redundant, so the optimizer has something useful to narrow on first
questions.explain: Since the negative condition itself can't be made selective, pairing it with a separate, genuinely selective condition (even if redundant from a pure business-logic standpoint) gives the optimizer something to narrow on before it evaluates the unselective part.
